claim: Ablation of descending LPNs in mice disturbs left-right coordination at high speeds without affecting fore-hind alternation.
source: Ablation of descending LPNs in mice disturbs left-right coordination at high speeds without affecting fore-hind alternation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work (Ruder et al., 2016) as referenced in the manuscript.

claim: The proposed CIN and diagonal LPN connections contribute to speed-dependent gait transition from walk, to trot, and then to gallop and bound.
source: The proposed CIN and diagonal LPN connections contribute to speed-dependent gait transition from walk, to trot, and then to gallop and bound
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational model presented in the manuscript, supported by simulation data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The homolateral LPN connections ensure fore-hind alternation in all gaits.
source: the homolateral LPN connections ensure fore-hind alternation in all gaits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational model, supported by simulation results.

claim: The model reproduces speed-dependent gait expression in intact and genetically transformed mice.
source: The model reproduces speed-dependent gait expression in intact and genetically transformed mice and the disruption of hindlimb coordination following ablation of descending LPNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figures 4, 5, and comparison with experimental data from Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015.

claim: The model reproduces the disruption of hindlimb coordination following ablation of descending LPNs.
source: The model reproduces speed-dependent gait expression in intact and genetically transformed mice and the disruption of hindlimb coordination following ablation of descending LPNs.
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figures 6 and 7, compared with experimental data from Ruder et al., 2016.

claim: Inputs to CINs and LPNs can affect interlimb coordination and change gait independent of speed.
source: Inputs to CINs and LPNs can affect interlimb coordination and change gait independent of speed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by model simulations shown in Figure 8G-I.

claim: CINs and LPNs represent the main targets for supraspinal and sensory afferent signals adjusting gait.
source: We suggest that these interneurons represent the main targets for supraspinal and sensory afferent signals adjusting gait.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on model predictions and supported by citations to experimental work showing these neurons receive such inputs.

claim: Mice change gait from walk to trot followed by gallop and bound as locomotor speed increases.
source: Mice change gait from walk to trot followed by gallop and bound as locomotor speed increases (Clarke and Still, 1999; Herbin et al., 2004; Herbin et al., 2007; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Lemieux et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Each gait is characterized by a distinct pattern of limb movements.
source: Each gait is characterized by a distinct pattern of limb movements (Hildebrand, 1989)
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Each limb is controlled by a separate central pattern generator (CPG).
source: It is generally accepted that each limb is controlled by a separate central pattern generator (CPGs), because cats are able to walk on split-belt treadmills with limbs stepping at different speeds (Forssberg et al., 1980; Halbertsma, 1983; Frigon et al., 2013, 2015; Thibaudier et al., 2013; Frigon, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies and represents established scientific consensus.

claim: Quadrupedal locomotion is controlled by four CPGs (one per limb) located in separate sections of the spinal cord.
source: Hence, quadrupedal locomotion is controlled by four CPGs (one per limb) located in separate sections of the spinal cord, specifically on the left and right side in the lumbar and cervical enlargements (Kato, 1990; Ballion et al., 2001; Juvin et al., 2005; Juvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The central control of interlimb coordination and gait expression is defined by neurons and neuronal pathways that mediate interactions between circuits controlling each limb.
source: Therefore, the central control of interlimb coordination and gait expression is defined by neurons and neuronal pathways that mediate interactions between circuits controlling each limb.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the concept that each limb has its own CPG.

claim: Interlimb pathways are mediated by short projecting commissural interneurons (CINs) that control left-right interactions at the lumbar and cervical levels.
source: These interlimb pathways are mediated by (a) short projecting commissural interneurons (CINs) that control left-right interactions at the lumbar and, presumably, cervical levels (Talpalar et al., 2013; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Molkov et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015; Danner et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental and modeling studies.

claim: Interlimb pathways are mediated by descending and ascending long propriospinal neurons (LPNs) that control homolateral and diagonal cervical-lumbar interactions.
source: and (b) descending (cervical-to-lumbar) and ascending (lumbar-to-cervical) long propriospinal neurons (LPNs) that control homolateral and diagonal cervical-lumbar interactions (Matsushita et al., 1979; Skinner et al., 1979, 1980; Menétrey et al., 1985; Nathan et al., 1996; Dutton et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Ruder et al., 2016; Flynn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Mutants lacking V0V CINs selectively lose trot.
source: Specifically, it was shown that mutants lacking V0V CINs selectively lose trot
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work (Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Kiehn, 2016).

claim: Mutants lacking both V0V and V0D CINs can only bound at any speed.
source: and mutants lacking both V0V and V0D CINs can only bound at any speed (Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: LPNs that directly couple the cervical and lumbar segments have been anatomically identified.
source: LPNs that directly couple the cervical and lumbar segments have been anatomically identified (Edinger, 1896; Nathan and Smith, 1959; Matsushita et al., 1979; Skinner et al., 1979; Skinner et al., 1980; Menétrey et al., 1985; Nathan et al., 1996; Dutton et al., 2006; Brockett et al., 2013; Flynn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Deletion of descending (cervical-to-lumbar) LPNs causes a speed-dependent distortion of left-right coordination.
source: In addition, Ruder et al. (2016) have shown that deletion of descending (cervical-to-lumbar) LPNs causes a speed-dependent distortion of left-right coordination.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: In locomotion induced by stimulation of the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), increasing the intensity of stimulation causes an increase of locomotor speed accompanied by sequential gait transitions.
source: In locomotion induced by stimulation of the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), increasing the intensity of stimulation causes an increase of locomotor speed accompanied by sequential gait transitions (Orlovskiĭ et al., 1966; Shik et al., 1966; Shik and Orlovsky, 1976; Skinner and Garcia-Rill, 1984; Grillner, 1985; Atsuta et al., 1990; Nicolopoulos-Stournaras and Iles, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The same brainstem drive that controls speed by exciting the rhythm generators also affects interlimb coordination by acting on CINs or LPNs.
source: From these observations, we hypothesized that the same brainstem drive that controls speed by exciting the rhythm generators also affects interlimb coordination by acting on CINs or LPNs (Danner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations and previous modeling work.

claim: Different CINs and LPNs receive supraspinal inputs.
source: This hypothesis is in accordance with multiple data confirming that different CINs and LPNs receive supraspinal inputs (Lloyd, 1942; Lloyd and McIntyre, 1948; Bannatyne et al., 2003; Jankowska et al., 2003; Cowley et al., 2010; Zaporozhets et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model consists of four rhythm generators (RGs), each controlling one limb.
source: The model consists of four rhythm generators (RGs), each controlling one limb (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: RGs interact via several bidirectional pathways mediated by CINs (left-right) and LPNs (homolateral and diagonal).
source: These RGs interact via several bidirectional pathways mediated by CINs (left-right) and LPNs (homolateral and diagonal).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Each RG consisted of a flexor (F) and extensor center (E) that mutually inhibited each other through intermediate inhibitory interneurons.
source: Each RG consisted of a flexor (F) and extensor center (E) that mutually inhibited each other through intermediate inhibitory interneurons (InF and InE, respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Under normal conditions extensor centers receive relatively high drive that keeps them in the regime of tonic activity.
source: Based on this concept and our previous models (Rybak et al., 2015; Molkov et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015; Danner et al., 2016; Ausborn et al., 2017), we assumed that under normal conditions extensor centers receive relatively high drive that keeps them in the regime of tonic activity.
evidence: This is an assumption based on previous modeling work and the concept of asymmetric flexion-dominated CPG organization.

claim: Extensor centers exhibited rhythmic bursting only due to rhythmic inhibition from the corresponding intrinsically oscillating flexor centers.
source: Hence, they exhibited rhythmic bursting only due to rhythmic inhibition from the corresponding intrinsically oscillating flexor centers.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior based on the model structure.

claim: The frequency of oscillation in the model was defined by the brainstem drive to flexor centers and was almost independent of the phasic interactions between RGs mediated by CINs and LPNs.
source: In this case, the frequency of oscillation in the model was defined by the brainstem drive to flexor centers and was almost independent of the phasic interactions between RGs mediated by CINs and LPNs (Rybak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of model behavior supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The inhibitory V0D CINs provide direct mutual inhibition between the left and right flexor centers.
source: the inhibitory V0D CINs provide direct mutual inhibition between the left and right flexor centers
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: The excitatory V0V CINs provide mutual inhibition between the flexor centers (receiving inputs from excitatory V2a and acting through inhibitory Ini neurons).
source: the excitatory V0V CINs also provide mutual inhibition between the flexor centers (receiving inputs from excitatory V2a and acting through inhibitory Ini neurons)
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: The excitatory V3 CINs provide mutual excitation between the flexor centers.
source: the excitatory V3 CINs provide mutual excitation between the flexor centers
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: The inhibitory CINi CINs provide inhibition from the extensor to the contralateral flexor centers.
source: and the inhibitory CINi CINs provide inhibition from the extensor to the contralateral flexor centers.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: There are excitatory and inhibitory descending LPNs.
source: Ruder et al. (2016) reported that there are excitatory and inhibitory descending LPNs
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Ascending LPNs are only excitatory.
source: whereas ascending LPNs are only excitatory.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work (Ruder et al., 2016).

claim: Both descending and ascending LPNs project homolaterally and diagonally.
source: Both descending and ascending LPNs project homolaterally and diagonally.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work (Ruder et al., 2016).

claim: There are more diagonal than homolateral excitatory LPNs.
source: There are more diagonal then homolateral excitatory LPNs
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work (Ruder et al., 2016).

claim: There are more homolateral than diagonal inhibitory LPNs.
source: while the opposite is the case for inhibitory LPNs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work (Ruder et al., 2016).

claim: The excitatory homolateral LPNs were identified as Shox2.
source: The excitatory homolateral LPNs were identified as Shox2
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work (Ruder et al., 2016).

claim: The excitatory diagonal LPNs were identified as V0V neurons.
source: and the excitatory diagonal LPNs as V0V neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work (Ruder et al., 2016).

claim: Diagonally projecting inhibitory LPNs are of V0D type.
source: We have hypothesized that diagonally projecting inhibitory LPNs are of V0D type.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The excitatory Shox2 neurons provide excitation from each cervical extensor to its homolateral lumbar flexor center.
source: the excitatory Shox2 neurons provide excitation from each cervical extensor to its homolateral lumbar flexor center
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Inhibitory LPNs of unidentified type (LPNi) provide inhibition from each cervical flexor to its homolateral lumbar flexor center.
source: inhibitory LPNs of unidentified type (LPNi) provide inhibition from each cervical flexor to its homolateral lumbar flexor center
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: V0V LPNs provide excitation from each cervical flexor to its diagonal flexor center.
source: V0V LPNs provide excitation from each cervical flexor to its diagonal flexor center
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Inhibitory V0D LPNs provide inhibition from each cervical flexor to its diagonal lumbar flexor center.
source: and inhibitory V0D LPNs provide inhibition from each cervical flexor to its diagonal lumbar flexor center.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lumbar-to-cervical connections mirror the excitatory cervical-to-lumbar connections but do not include inhibitory LPNs.
source: Lumbar-to-cervical connections (Figure 2C) mirror the excitatory cervical-to-lumbar connections but do not include inhibitory LPNs.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: One brainstem drive excited flexor centers and inhibited the local V0 CINs at cervical and lumbar levels and the descending diagonal V0D LPNs.
source: Finally, there were two brainstem drives (Figure 2D): one that excited flexor centers and inhibited the local V0 CINs at cervical and lumbar levels and the descending diagonal V0D LPNs, promoting left-right and diagonal alternation between the corresponding RGs
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Another brainstem drive provided constant excitatory drive to the extensor centers.
source: and the other that provided constant excitatory drive to the extensor centers.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The increase in frequency occurred mostly due to shortening of the extension phase, while the flexion phase remained almost constant.
source: This increase in frequency occurred mostly due to shortening of the extension phase, while the flexion phase remained almost constant (Figure 4B, bottom diagram)
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4B, which is consistent with experimental observations.

claim: Shortening of extension phase while flexion phase remains constant is a characteristic property of fictive and real locomotion across species.
source: which is a characteristic property of fictive and real locomotion across species (Halbertsma, 1983; Hildebrand, 1989; Frigon and Gossard, 2009; Danner et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The increased frequency in the model was accompanied by sequential gait changes from walk to trot to gallop and then bound.
source: The increased frequency in the model was accompanied by sequential gait changes from walk to trot to gallop and then bound (Figure 4A) consistent with experimental observations (Figure 4C, Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4A, consistent with experimental data.

claim: The expressed walking gait was a lateral-sequence walk.
source: The expressed walking gait was a lateral-sequence walk (Figure 4A,D)
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: In lateral-sequence walk, flexion phases proceeded in the following order: hind-right, fore-right, hind-left and fore-left.
source: in which flexion phases proceeded in the following order: hind-right, fore-right, hind-left and fore-left.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior during walk.

claim: Walk occurred at frequencies from 2 to 4 Hz.
source: This walk occurred at frequencies from 2 to 4 Hz (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At low frequencies during walk, the extension phase was three to four times longer than the flexion phase duration.
source: At low frequencies, the extension phase was three to four times longer than the flexion phase duration
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: During walk, the homolateral and diagonal phase differences were close to 0.25 and 0.75, respectively.
source: and the homolateral and diagonal phase differences were close to 0.25 and 0.75, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Trot was characterized by diagonal synchronization, left-right alternation and fore-hind alternation.
source: Trot (Figure 4A,E) was characterized by diagonal synchronization, left-right alternation and fore-hind alternation.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Trot was expressed over a large range of frequencies (from 4 to 10.5 Hz).
source: It was expressed over a large range of frequencies (from 4 to 10.5 Hz; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gallops are characterized by synchronization or quasi-synchronization of the hind RGs and a non-zero phase difference between the fore RGs.
source: Gallops are characterized by synchronization or quasi-synchronization of the hind RGs and a non-zero phase difference between the fore RGs.
evidence: This is a description of gallop characteristics based on model behavior.

claim: In the model, gallop was expressed at frequencies between 9 and 11 Hz.
source: In the model (Figure 4A,B,F), gallop was expressed at frequencies between 9 and 11 Hz
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The model expressed transverse but not rotary gallops.
source: Thus, transverse but not rotary gallops were expressed.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: Some of the gallops exhibited an interval between the end of the hind extension and the beginning of the fore extension, in which all RGs were in flexion at the same time, corresponding to an aerial phase.
source: Some of the gallops exhibited an interval between the end of the hind extension and the beginning of the fore extension, in which all RGs were in flexion at the same time (Figure 4F). This corresponds to an aerial phase, characteristic for gallops.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Bound was characterized by left-right synchronization at cervical and lumbar levels, and homolateral and diagonal alternation.
source: Bound (Figure 4A,B,G) was characterized by left-right synchronization at cervical and lumbar levels, and homolateral and diagonal alternation.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Bound was expressed at frequencies between 11 and 12 Hz.
source: Bound was expressed at frequencies between 11 and 12 Hz.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: During bound, the flexion phase duration was always longer than the extension phase duration.
source: The flexion phase duration was always longer than the extension phase duration (Figure 4B, bottom diagram).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The frequency ranges, phase differences, and step cycle compositions of all gaits in the model were consistent with mouse locomotion.
source: The frequency ranges, phase differences, and step cycle compositions (relative phase durations) of all gaits were consistent with mouse locomotion (Figure 4B–G; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; see gait definitions in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data.

claim: At the lowest values of brainstem drive, both left-right and diagonal alternation promoting pathways dominated.
source: At the lowest values of brainstem drive, both left-right (local V0D and V0V CINs) and diagonal alternation (diagonal V0D LPNs) promoting pathways dominated.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior at low drive values.

claim: The transition from trot to gallop and bound was governed by brainstem-drive-controlled speed-dependent changes in the left-right and diagonal pathways.
source: The transition from trot to gallop and bound was governed by brainstem-drive-controlled speed-dependent changes in the left-right and diagonal pathways.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism underlying gait transitions in the model.

claim: The left-right alternation promoting local CINs (V0D and V0V) received inhibition from the brainstem that increased with speed.
source: The left-right alternation promoting local CINs (V0D and V0V) received inhibition from the brainstem that increased with speed
evidence: This is a description of the model structure and its effect on behavior.

claim: The left-right synchronization promoting local CINs (V3 and CINi) did not receive brainstem inhibition.
source: while the left-right synchronization promoting local CINs (V3 and CINi) did not receive brainstem inhibition (Figure 2D, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure shown in Figures 2D and 3.

claim: With increasing brainstem drive (and frequency), the pathway promoting left-right synchronization became stronger than those promoting left-right alternation, resulting in a transition from trot to gallop and then to bound.
source: Thus, with increasing brainstem drive (and frequency), the pathway promoting left-right synchronization became stronger than those promoting left-right alternation. This resulted in a transition from trot to gallop and then to bound (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of model behavior shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The diagonally projecting V0V LPNs, promoting diagonal synchronization, acted synergistically with local V0V CINs.
source: The diagonally projecting V0V LPNs, promoting diagonal synchronization, acted synergistically with local V0V CINs.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior.

claim: The bifurcation from trot to gallop resembled a subcritical (backwards) pitchfork bifurcation in the hind (and fore) left-right phase differences.
source: The bifurcation from trot to gallop resembled a subcritical (backwards) pitchfork bifurcation in the hind (and fore) left-right phase differences.
evidence: This is a mathematical characterization of the model behavior.

claim: Hysteresis is a common feature of gait transitions in quadrupeds.
source: Such a hysteresis is a common feature of gait transitions in quadrupeds (Heglund and Taylor, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The addition of diagonal LPNs in the present model was critical for stable gallop to exist.
source: Note, that the previous model (Danner et al., 2016) could not reproduce stable gallops; they only existed as a transitional regime. Therefore, the addition of diagonal LPNs in the present model was critical for stable gallop to exist.
evidence: This is a comparison with the previous model and a conclusion about the importance of diagonal LPNs.

claim: When all V0V neurons were deleted in the model, only walk, gallop and bound were expressed; trot was selectively lost.
source: When all V0V neurons were deleted (Figure 5B) only walk, gallop and bound were expressed; trot was selectively lost.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Deletion of V2a had the same effect as deletion of V0V, because V2a relayed all inputs to V0V CINs and LPNs.
source: Deletion of V2a had the same effect as deletion of V0V, because V2a relayed all inputs to V0V CINs and LPNs.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations and an explanation based on model structure.

claim: Deletion of both V0V and V0D resulted in the removal of all left-right alternation promoting pathways and caused the loss of all alternating gaits.
source: Deletion of both V0V and V0D resulted in the removal of all left-right alternation promoting pathways and caused the loss of all alternating gaits (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: After deletion of both V0V and V0D, bound was stable over all frequencies.
source: Bound was stable over all frequencies.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations after deletion of V0V and V0D.

claim: Deletion of descending LPNs influences left-right coordination: at low speeds both the fore and hind limbs were alternating, then at medium speeds the hind limbs, and at high speeds both the fore and hind limbs demonstrated disturbed coordination.
source: Ruder et al. (2016) showed that deletion of descending LPNs influences left-right coordination: at low speeds both the fore and hind limbs were alternating, then at medium speeds the hind limbs, and at high speeds both the fore and hind limbs demonstrated disturbed coordination with both alternating and synchronized activities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: In the model, deletion of the cervical-to-lumbar LPNs resulted in the emergence of new stable states.
source: In our model, deletion of the cervical-to-lumbar LPNs resulted in the emergence of new stable states (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: After deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs, at low brainstem drive values walk remained the only stable state.
source: At low brainstem drive values walk remained the only stable state and with increasing drive it gradually transitioned towards trot.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations after deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs.

claim: The disturbance of the fore and hind left-right phase differences after deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs was mainly caused by the deletion of diagonally projecting V0V LPNs.
source: Thus, the disturbance of the fore and hind left-right phase differences was mainly caused by the deletion of diagonally projecting V0V LPNs.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing model results after different deletions.

claim: The remaining homolaterally projecting LPNs maintained fore-hind alternation after deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs.
source: The remaining homolaterally projecting LPNs maintained fore-hind alternation after deletion.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: Local V0V CINs maintained the stable branch of left-right alternation after deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs.
source: Local V0V CINs maintained the stable branch of left-right alternation.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations.

claim: Deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs resulted in the emergence of new, additional stable states at medium and high brainstem drive values.
source: In the above section, we described that deletion of the cervical-to-lumbar LPNs resulted in the emergence of new, additional stable states at medium and high brainstem drive values.
evidence: This is a summary of results from model simulations.

claim: In the intact model with increased noise, at medium brainstem drives the increased noise caused phase durations and phase differences to become more variable, but both the fore and hind RGs remained alternating over all steps.
source: In the intact model, at medium brainstem drives (related to trot), the increased noise caused phase durations and phase differences to become more variable, but both, the fore and hind RGs remained alternating over all steps (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations with noise shown in Figure 7A.

claim: After deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs with increased noise, the applied noise caused spontaneous transitions between the steady states: the activity of hind RGs was spontaneously switching between synchronization and alternation while the fore RGs remained alternating.
source: After deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs, the applied noise caused spontaneous transitions between the steady states: the activity of hind RGs was spontaneously switching between synchronization and alternation while the fore RGs remained alternating (see dashed box in Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations with noise shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A similar disruption of interlimb coordination has been described in mice after deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs.
source: A similar disruption of interlimb coordination has been described in mice after deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs (Ruder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The model reproduced the speed-dependent effect of changes in the proportion of appropriate and misaligned steps after deletion of cervical-to-lumbar LPNs: at low speeds hind and fore limb coordination remained appropriate for trot, at medium speeds hind limb coordination was disturbed, and at high speeds both fore and hind limb coordination was affected.
source: Furthermore, the model also reproduced the speed-dependent effect of changes in the proportion of appropriate and misaligned steps: at low speeds hind and fore limb coordination remained appropriate for trot, at medium speeds hind limb coordination was disturbed, and at high speeds both fore and hind limb coordination was affected (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 7C-E, consistent with experimental data.

claim: Mice usually switch gaits and locomotor speeds abruptly with few or no intermediary steps.
source: Mice usually switch gaits and locomotor speeds abruptly with few or no intermediary steps (Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Transitions from walk to trot, from gallop to trot and from walk to gallop and back to walk in the model usually required only one or two cycles to stabilize the new gait and locomotor frequency.
source: Transitions from walk to trot, from gallop to trot and from walk to gallop and back to walk (Figure 8A–C) mirrored experimental observations closely (Figure 8D–E; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015): they usually required only one or two cycles to stabilize the new gait and locomotor frequency.
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8A-C, consistent with experimental data.

claim: Additional inhibitory drive to all V0V CINs and LPNs during trot induced a transition to bound without significantly affecting the frequency.
source: For example, additional inhibition to V0V CINs and LPNs during trot induced a transition to bound without significantly affecting the frequency, resulting in a bound at a frequency characteristic of trot (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Excitatory drive to the local V0V CINs during gallop induced a transition to trot, without significantly affecting speed.
source: Excitatory drive to the local V0V CINs during gallop induced a transition to trot, again without significantly affecting speed (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Excitation of the local cervical V0V CINs during gallop caused the fore left-right phase differences to move farther from synchronization while the hind RG coordination remained almost unchanged.
source: Excitation of the local cervical V0V CINs during gallop caused the fore left-right phase differences to move farther from synchronization and the left and right extension phases of the fore RGs to overlap less, while the hind RG coordination remained almost unchanged (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is a result from model simulations shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Tonic inputs to CINs and LPNs were able to alter interlimb coordination and gait almost independently of frequency.
source: Thus, tonic inputs to CINs and LPNs were able to alter interlimb coordination and gait almost independently of frequency.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations shown in Figure 8G-I.

claim: The drive to the extensor centers may represent a separate descending supraspinal drive to extensor circuits operating through the medial reticulospinal or vestibulospinal tracts and/or inputs from cutaneous afferents and load receptors from extensor muscles.
source: This drive may represent a separate descending supraspinal drive to extensor circuits operating through the medial reticulospinal or vestibulospinal tracts and/or inputs from cutaneous afferents and load receptors from extensor muscles (Hiebert and Pearson, 1999; Dietz and Duysens, 2000; Bouyer and Rossignol, 2003; Rossignol et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about what the model drive might represent, supported by citations.

claim: The brainstem drive to the flexor centers put them into a rhythmic bursting regime.
source: The brainstem drive to the flexor centers put them into a rhythmic bursting regime
evidence: This is a description of model behavior.

claim: Strong inhibition between flexor and extensor centers mediated by inhibitory interneurons caused rhythmic flexor-extensor alternation.
source: and strong inhibition between flexor and extensor centers mediated by inhibitory interneurons caused rhythmic flexor-extensor alternation (Zhang et al., 2014; Britz et al., 2015; Rybak et al., 2015; Shevtsova et al., 2015; Danner et al., 2016; Shevtsova and Rybak, 2016).
evidence: This is a description of model behavior supported by citations.

claim: Progressive increase of brainstem drive to flexor centers increased locomotor frequency.
source: Progressive increase of this drive increased locomotor frequency
evidence: This is a description of model behavior.

claim: Gait transitions are caused by brainstem drives acting on neurons coupling the RGs and affecting the balance between the activities of pathways promoting synchronization and alternation.
source: Following our previous model (Danner et al., 2016), we suggest that gait transitions are caused by brainstem drives acting on neurons coupling the RGs and affecting the balance between the activities of pathways promoting synchronization and alternation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the model and previous work.

claim: Spinal CINs and LPNs receive excitatory and inhibitory inputs from supraspinal structures.
source: Multiple studies confirm that spinal CINs and LPNs receive excitatory and inhibitory inputs from supraspinal structures (Skinner et al., 1979; Skinner et al., 1980; Alstermark et al., 1987; Bannatyne et al., 2003; Jankowska et al., 2003; Jankowska et al., 2005; Jankowska et al., 2006; Matsuyama et al., 2004; Cowley et al., 2008; Cowley et al., 2010; Jankowska, 2008; Szokol et al., 2011; Zaporozhets et al., 2011; Juvin et al., 2012; Mitchell et al., 2016; Ruder et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: CINs and LPNs receive direct and indirect input from sensory afferents.
source: This is consistent with multiple experimental data showing that CINs and LPNs receive direct and indirect input from sensory afferents (Lloyd and McIntyre, 1948; Edgley et al., 2003; Bannatyne et al., 2006; Jankowska et al., 2009; Flynn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Afferent feedback from each limb projects mostly to the spinal cord section controlling the same limb.
source: In accord with this is the notion that afferent feedback from each limb projects mostly to the spinal cord section controlling the same limb (Frigon, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The influence of afferent feedback on spinal circuits and RGs controlling other limbs should be mostly mediated by CINs and LPNs located in the section receiving the feedback.
source: and hence its influence on spinal circuits and RGs controlling other limbs should be mostly mediated by CINs and LPNs located in this section.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the anatomical organization.

claim: CINs and LPNs represent the main neural targets for different local/intraspinal, supraspinal, and sensory inputs to control interlimb coordination and adjust gait to various internal and external conditions.
source: Therefore, we suggest that CINs and LPNs represent the main neural targets for different local/intraspinal, supraspinal, and sensory inputs to control interlimb coordination and adjust gait to various internal and external conditions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on model predictions and anatomical/physiological data.

claim: Separate (independent of brainstem drives) signals to CINs and LPNs only (e.g. from sensory afferents) can affect limb coordination and change gait independent of speed.
source: Separate (independent of brainstem drives) signals to CINs and LPNs only (e.g. from sensory afferents) can affect limb coordination and change gait independent of speed (as shown in Figure 8G–I).
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations shown in Figure 8G-I.

claim: Mechanical coupling between the limbs and body can influence interlimb coordination and interact with the neural control.
source: Mechanical coupling between the limbs and body can also influence interlimb coordination and interact with the neural control (Nishikawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Gaits are not only characterized by the phase differences between the limbs but also by a change in kinematics and muscle activation patterns.
source: Moreover, gaits are not only characterized by the phase differences between the limbs but also by a change in kinematics and muscle activation patterns (Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Diagonal V0D LPNs ensure stable walk.
source: Walk and the transition to trot: diagonal V0D LPNs ensure stable walk
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations and analysis.

claim: Diagonal V0V LPNs stabilize trot.
source: Trot and the transition to gallop and bound: diagonal V0V LPNs stabilize trot
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations and analysis.

claim: Diagonal V0D LPNs support walk.
source: The model proposes the following roles for LPNs: diagonal V0D LPNs supports walk
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations.

claim: Diagonal V0V LPNs together with local V0V CINs stabilize trot.
source: diagonal V0V LPNs together with local V0V CINs stabilize trot
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations.

claim: Homolateral LPNs ensure fore-hind alternation in all gaits.
source: and homolateral LPNs ensure fore-hind alternation in all gaits.
evidence: This is a conclusion from model simulations.

claim: The lateral-sequence walk is the preferred walk of several quadrupeds, including mice, dogs, cats, and humans crawling.
source: which is the preferred walk of several quadrupeds, including mice, dogs, cats, and humans crawling (Patrick et al., 2009; Bellardita and Kiehn, 2015; Righetti et al., 2015; Frigon, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.
